\chapter{Hair, Ear, and Throat}
\label{ch:hi-body-more}
\hlchaptermodality{46}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name five more parts of the body in Hindi, and follow the wearing-down that turned each Sanskrit word into the one people say.}

Complete HI-C46-throat and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[bāl]{\hi{बाल} (bāl) — hair}

\label{lesson:HI-C46-hair}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run of words: what did \emph{namak} mean, and what did \emph{sābun} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{बाल}}
\textbf{\hi{बाल}} (\emph{bāl}) — \textquotedblleft{}hair\textquotedblright{}.

One hair, and by extension all the hair on a head. Sanskrit \emph{vāla}, a hair or a horse's tail, stands behind it, and the turn from \emph{v-} to \emph{b-} is regular enough between Sanskrit and Hindi that you can use it as a rule of thumb.

Take care with its neighbour: \emph{bāl-} also means 'child' in words borrowed straight from Sanskrit, as in \emph{bālak}. Those are two different words that happened to fall together in sound, and only the sentence around them says which one is meant.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five more body words.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bāl}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{bāl}, then \emph{sābun}, so the washing and the washed sit together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{बाल} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}hair\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[uṅglī]{\hi{उँगली} (uṅglī) — a finger}

\label{lesson:HI-C46-finger}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{bāl} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{उँगली}}
\textbf{\hi{उँगली}} (\emph{uṅglī}) — \textquotedblleft{}a finger\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{aṅgulī}, a finger, built on \emph{aṅga}, 'a limb'. That one root supports a whole small household of hand-words: \emph{aṅgūṭhā} is the thumb and \emph{aṅgūṭhī} is the ring that goes on it.

The mark above the line here is doing the work the \emph{ṅ} used to do. The nasal consonant dissolved into the vowel and left only the little moon-and-dot behind, which is the same trade you already saw inside \emph{pāṁch}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two of five.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{uṅglī}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{uṅglī}, then \emph{bāl}, and touch each as you name it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{उँगली} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a finger\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kān]{\hi{कान} (kān) — an ear}

\label{lesson:HI-C46-ear}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{uṅglī} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{कान}}
\textbf{\hi{कान}} (\emph{kān}) — \textquotedblleft{}an ear\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{karṇa}, the ear — also the name of the warrior in the Mahabharata who was born wearing earrings. The path to \hi{कान} is the ordinary one: the \emph{-rṇ-} cluster collapses, the vowel that survives it lengthens, and a two-syllable word becomes one.

The same collapse is what turned \emph{suvarṇa}, 'good colour', into \emph{sonā}, gold. Once you have seen it twice it stops looking like an accident and starts looking like the machine it is.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three: hair, a finger, an ear.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kān}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{kān}, then \emph{uṅglī}, then \emph{bāl}, back down the run
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{कान} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}an ear\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nāk]{\hi{नाक} (nāk) — a nose}

\label{lesson:HI-C46-nose}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kān} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{नाक}}
\textbf{\hi{नाक}} (\emph{nāk}) — \textquotedblleft{}a nose\textquotedblright{}.

From Sanskrit \emph{nāsikā}, 'nostril', by way of Prakrit — and \emph{nāsikā} is a cousin of Latin \emph{nāsus} and of English \textquotedblleft{}nose\textquotedblright{}, which makes this one of the clearest family resemblances anywhere on the body.

Hindi puts the nose where English puts the face: to have your \hi{नाक} cut is to be humiliated, and to keep it high is to keep your honour. The idiom is old enough that the literal sense has stopped showing through.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four, and the last one is on the inside.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{nāk}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{nāk}, then \emph{kān}, so the two openings of the head sit together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{नाक} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a nose\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[galā]{\hi{गला} (galā) — the throat}

\label{lesson:HI-C46-throat}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{nāk} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{गला}}
\textbf{\hi{गला}} (\emph{galā}) — \textquotedblleft{}the throat\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{gala}, the throat, a cousin of Latin \emph{gula}, the gullet — the word English took twice over, once as \textquotedblleft{}gullet\textquotedblright{} and once, by a longer road, as \textquotedblleft{}gluttony\textquotedblright{}.

Hindi keeps the plain sense and adds the obvious extension: your \hi{गला} is also your voice, and to say that it has gone is to say you have gone hoarse. The organ and what comes out of it share one word, which is a bargain most languages strike somewhere.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five, and the run is closed: hair, a finger, an ear, a nose, the throat.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{galā}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order — \emph{bāl}, \emph{uṅglī}, \emph{kān}, \emph{nāk}, \emph{galā}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{गला} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}the throat\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
